title: Heat Break Compliance Pocket
oneLiner: A field supervisor pocket app that turns heat-wave rules, breaks, symptoms, and photos into a defensible jobsite log.
targetUser: Small construction crews, landscapers, warehouse leads, outdoor event supervisors, restaurant patio managers, and field-service owners without dedicated EHS staff.
keyUX: Start a shift, log forecast and workload, trigger break/water/shade reminders, capture symptom checks and photos, and export a daily heat-safety proof log.
sourceSignals: S9 - Cal/OSHA heat illness reminder during heat wave, 2026: https://www.dir.ca.gov/DIRNews/2026/2026-25.html
S10 - OSHA heat exposure guidance, current: https://www.osha.gov/heat-exposure
stitchPrompt: Create a responsive mobile-first web app called "Heat Break Compliance Pocket" for small construction crews, landscapers, warehouse leads, outdoor event supervisors, restaurant patio managers, and field-service owners without dedicated EHS staff. The app is based on observed user pull: supervisors already juggle heat advisories, water and shade rules, symptom checks, toolbox talks, crew acclimatization, and proof logs during hotter workdays. The app should use a shift log with proof stamps mechanic around the trigger moment "a hot shift starts and the supervisor must prove prevention happened" and make the first screen communicate "Today's heat risk needs proof, not memory." Use the user's own language: "I need a simple log that proves we gave breaks before someone gets sick." Build the core workflow around forecast, work type, crew roster, acclimatization, water/shade access, break schedule, symptom checks, photos, and incident notes, and produce a daily heat-safety proof log. Required sections: heat risk shift header, crew acclimatization roster, water shade and break timeline, symptom check cards, indoor/outdoor workload slider, photo and toolbox-talk proof, incident escalation button, and daily compliance log export. Emotional pressure to make visible: 건강, worker trust, inspection anxiety, and the cost of ignoring symptoms. Design direction: use the `field-ops` profile with glove-friendly mobile controls, high-contrast heat states, rugged white and steel cards, big timers, and photo-proof tiles. Avoid generic dashboard framing; make the main interaction feel like a pocket foreman log used while walking the jobsite.
